**Circuit:** The AC mains is applied to the primary of a transformer. One end A of the secondary coil AB is joined to the anode of a single junction diode D; the cathode of D goes to one end X of the load resistance \(R_{L}\), and the other end Y of \(R_{L}\) is returned to the other end B of the secondary. The output is taken across \(R_{L}\). (See the circuit diagram accompanying this answer.)

The transformer serves two purposes: it lets the AC input be stepped up or stepped down as the circuit requires, and it isolates the rectifier from the mains supply, reducing the risk of shock.

**Working:** The AC voltage across the secondary AB reverses its polarity every half cycle.

1. *Positive half cycle:* point A is at a higher potential than point B, so the diode D is forward biased. It behaves as a closed switch, conducts, and current flows through \(R_{L}\) from X to Y. A voltage appears across the load.

2. *Negative half cycle:* point A is at a lower potential than point B, so D is reverse biased. It behaves as an open switch and does not conduct. No current passes through \(R_{L}\) and the output voltage is zero.

Thus the diode conducts only during the alternate positive half cycles and blocks the current during the negative half cycles. Current through \(R_{L}\) is therefore always in the same direction, and the DC output across \(R_{L}\) is a series of alternate pulses — one pulse for every complete cycle of the input. Because only one of the two half cycles is used, this is called a half wave rectifier, and its maximum efficiency is only 40.6%.

**Frequency of the ripple:** one output pulse is produced for each input cycle, so the ripple frequency of a half wave rectifier is **equal to the frequency of the AC input**. For the 50 Hz mains supply the ripple frequency is 50 Hz.

The output of a rectifier is not steady DC. It is a train of unidirectional pulses, so along with the DC component it always contains a small AC component. This AC component in the DC output of a rectifier is called the **ripple**.

The ripple is undesirable: it makes the output voltage fluctuate instead of holding a steady value, and the effectiveness of a rectifier is judged by how small this ripple is, measured by the ripple factor

\(\text{Ripple factor} = \dfrac{\text{r.m.s. value of AC component}}{\text{value of DC component}}\)

Most electronic gadgets — a TV, a mobile charger and so on — need a steady DC supply and will not work properly on a fluctuating one.

A **filter** is a circuit which removes the AC component (the ripple) from the rectifier output and allows only the DC component to pass. Its output is almost pure DC. Hence a filter is needed in a power supply to convert the pulsating output of the rectifier into a nearly steady DC voltage, which is then set to the required value by a voltage regulator.

**Circuit:** A full wave rectifier uses a **centre-tapped transformer** and **two** diodes. The two ends A and B of the centre-tapped secondary are connected to the anodes of the diodes \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) respectively. The cathodes of both diodes are joined together at the point X, which is one end of the load resistance \(R_{L}\); the other end of \(R_{L}\) is returned to the centre tap of the secondary. The output is taken across \(R_{L}\). (See the circuit diagram accompanying this answer.)

**Working:** The diodes are connected so that they conduct alternately, one in each half cycle.

1. *Positive half cycle:* the point A is at a higher potential than the point B. The diode \(D_{1}\) is forward biased and conducts, while \(D_{2}\) is reverse biased and does not. Current flows from A through \(D_{1}\), through \(R_{L}\), and back to the centre tap.

2. *Negative half cycle:* the polarity reverses, so the point B is now at a higher potential than the point A. Now \(D_{2}\) is forward biased and conducts while \(D_{1}\) is reverse biased. Current flows from B through \(D_{2}\), through \(R_{L}\), and back to the centre tap.

In both half cycles the current passes through the load resistance **in the same direction**, so the voltage across \(R_{L}\) is unidirectional throughout the input cycle.

**Advantages:** rectification takes place in both half cycles of the AC input, and the ripple in a full wave rectifier is less than that in a half wave rectifier. Two output pulses are obtained for every input cycle, so the ripple frequency is twice the input frequency (100 Hz for a 50 Hz supply). The maximum efficiency of a full wave rectifier is 81.2%, which is twice that of a half wave rectifier.

A Zener diode of breakdown voltage \(V_{Z}\) is connected in **reverse bias** across the unregulated input \(V_{in}\) (with \(V_{in} > V_{Z}\)) through a series resistance \(R_{S}\). The load \(R_{L}\) is connected **in parallel** with the Zener diode, so the voltage across the load is always the same as the voltage across the diode.

The key property used is that once the diode is in the breakdown region, the voltage across it stays almost constant at \(V_{Z}\) however much the current through it changes. The series resistance \(R_{S}\) both limits the diode current and absorbs whatever voltage is left over. There are three cases:

**(a) Input voltage increases.** The current through \(R_{S}\) and through the Zener diode increases, so the voltage drop across \(R_{S}\) increases. But the voltage across the diode does not change, because it is in the breakdown region. \(R_{S}\) has absorbed the whole of the increase, and the output voltage across the load stays constant.

**(b) Load resistance decreases (load current increases).** The extra load current cannot come from the source, because the drop across \(R_{S}\) does not change while the Zener stays within its regulating range. Instead the Zener current \(I_{Z}\) decreases by exactly the same amount, so that the total current stays the same. The output voltage again stays constant.

**(c) No load (\(R_{L} = \infty\)).** The load current is zero and the whole circuit current passes through the Zener diode, which then dissipates maximum power. \(R_{S}\) is chosen so that even in this worst case the maximum power rating \(P_{Z} = I_{Z(\max)} V_{Z}\) of the diode is not exceeded.

Hence a regulated DC output voltage \(V_{O} = V_{Z}\) is obtained across \(R_{L}\) for all input voltages between a minimum and a maximum, and for all load currents within the diode's regulating range. The Zener diode thus acts as a voltage regulator.

The I-V characteristic of a Zener diode is drawn with the forward current \(I_{F}\) and forward voltage \(V_{F}\) in the first quadrant, and the reverse current \(-I_{R}\) and reverse voltage \(-V_{R}\) in the third quadrant.

**Forward characteristic.** In forward bias a Zener diode behaves exactly like an ordinary p-n junction diode. Almost no current flows until the applied voltage reaches the knee (cut-in) voltage, about 0.3 V for germanium and 0.7 V for silicon. Beyond the knee the current rises very steeply for a small further increase in voltage, so the forward branch is a sharply rising exponential-looking curve. Nothing about the forward branch is special to a Zener diode, and this is not the region in which it is used.

**Reverse characteristic.** In reverse bias only a very small, almost constant reverse saturation current flows at first, so the curve runs nearly flat and close to the voltage axis. When the reverse voltage reaches the Zener voltage \(V_{Z}\), breakdown occurs: covalent bonds at the narrow junction are broken by the strong junction field, a large number of free carriers become available, and the reverse current increases very sharply. On the graph the curve turns and drops almost vertically. Along this vertical portion — the **Zener breakdown region** — the current changes from \(I_{Z(\min)}\) to \(I_{Z(\max)}\) while the voltage across the diode stays essentially constant at \(V_{Z}\).

Because the diode is heavily doped, this breakdown occurs at a low reverse voltage and, unlike an ordinary diode, it does **not** damage the diode, provided the current is kept below \(I_{Z(\max)}\) by a series resistance. It is precisely this constant-voltage vertical portion of the reverse characteristic that makes the Zener diode useful as a voltage regulator.

A Light Emitting Diode is a p-n junction diode which emits light when a large forward current is passed through it. In its construction the n-region is more heavily doped than the p-region, and the junction is encased in a dome-shaped transparent epoxy case so that the light escapes uniformly in all directions and internal reflections are minimised.

**Working:** The LED is connected in **forward bias**. The forward bias lowers the potential barrier, so electrons are injected from the n-side into the junction region and holes from the p-side. Near the junction an electron from the conduction band recombines with a hole in the valence band. In this recombination the electron falls from the higher-energy conduction band to the lower-energy valence band, and the energy difference — essentially the band gap \(E_{g}\) — is released as a photon:

\(E_{g} = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)

The photons are all of nearly the same energy, so the light emitted is monochromatic (a single colour). Because the recombination is arranged to take place in a thin layer at the surface, a large fraction of these photons can leave the junction instead of being reabsorbed in the material.

The number of recombinations per second is proportional to the forward current, so the light output is directly proportional to the forward current: the larger the forward current, the brighter the LED. Since the LED starts conducting only after its cut-in voltage is reached (about 1.5 V to 3.5 V, much more than for an ordinary diode) and its current rating is only a few tens of milliamperes, a suitable resistance must always be connected in series with it to limit the current.

The colour depends on the band gap of the compound semiconductor used: AlGaAs gives infrared, GaAsP red or yellow, AlGaP red or green and ZnSe blue.

**Construction.** A solar cell is a large-area p-n junction. The thin n-side faces the incoming solar radiation and the relatively thick p-side forms the back of the cell. Both faces are coated with a conducting material to serve as electrodes: the contact on the n-side is the **front contact** and the one on the p-side is the **back (rear) contact**. Over the n-side there is an **antireflection coating**, which allows visible light to pass into the cell but reflects the infrared (heat) radiation, protecting the cell from heating — necessary because the electronic properties of semiconductors are sensitive to temperature. The n-side is kept thin so that the light entering it reaches the depletion region, where the electron-hole pairs are generated. The load is connected between the front and the rear contacts.

The material used must (i) be photosensitive, absorbing light and raising electrons to a higher energy state, and (ii) allow those higher-energy electrons to be taken out into an external circuit. Its band gap should lie between about 1.0 eV and 1.8 eV, it should have high optical absorption and good electrical conductivity, and it should be easily available. Silicon (\(E_{g} = 1.1\) eV) is the material most commonly used; GaAs (1.43 eV), CdTe (1.45 eV) and CuInSe (1.04 eV) are also used.

**Working.** When light is incident on the cell:
1. Photons whose energy is greater than the band gap are absorbed and generate electron-hole pairs in the depletion region of the p-n junction. These are the photo-generated carriers.
2. The intrinsic electric field of the depletion region separates them before they can recombine: a light-generated electron in the p-region that reaches the junction is swept across into the n-region, and a light-generated hole is swept into the p-region.
3. Positive charge therefore accumulates on the p-region and negative charge on the n-region, and the cell develops a voltage across it. The electrons are collected at the cathode and the holes at the anode.
4. When an external circuit is connected across the contacts, these light-generated carriers flow through it, and the power produced is dissipated (utilised) in the load resistance.

The I-V characteristic is drawn in the fourth quadrant because the cell supplies current to the load. Its intercept on the current axis is the short-circuit current \(I_{sc}\) and its intercept on the voltage axis is the open-circuit voltage \(V_{oc}\); the power delivered is zero at both of these, and is maximum at an intermediate point called the maximum power point.

A photodiode is a special p-n junction diode which converts light energy into electrical energy; it is also called a photodetector or photosensor. Its junction is enclosed in a glass window so that only the junction is exposed to light, the rest of the diode being painted with an opaque colour or covered. It is always operated in **reverse biased** mode.

**Principle of operation.**

1. In reverse bias, and in the dark, only a very small reverse saturation current flows. It is carried by the minority carriers on either side of the junction, and it depends only on the concentration of the minority carriers, not on the applied voltage. Since it flows even when the diode is not illuminated it is called the **dark current**.

2. When the junction is illuminated by photons whose energy is greater than the band gap of the semiconductor, electron-hole pairs are generated in the depletion region.

3. These electrons and holes are separated by the intrinsic electric field present in the depletion region: the electrons are attracted towards the anode and the holes towards the cathode. More carriers are thus available for conduction and the reverse current increases.

4. The number of pairs generated per second is proportional to the number of photons arriving per second, so **the reverse current of a photodiode depends on the intensity of the incident light** and varies linearly with it. The reverse current is thus controlled by controlling the concentration of the minority carriers at the junction.

5. As the intensity is increased the reverse current increases, and beyond a certain point it becomes constant; this constant value is the **saturation current** of the photodiode. The total current through the device is the sum of this photocurrent and the dark current, so the sensitivity of the device is improved by minimising the dark current.

A related parameter is the **dark resistance**, the resistance of the photodiode when it is not illuminated:

\(R_{d} = \dfrac{\text{Maximum reverse voltage}}{\text{Dark current}}\)
